SK2161 The DateTime has no time zone and is converted as if it had one

A DateTime built by a constructor that takes no DateTimeKind — so its Kind is Unspecified — is passed to ToUniversalTime, ToLocalTime or a DateTimeOffset conversion, each of which has to invent the offset it was never given.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since2.0
SupersedesS6562, S6563, S6566

Why

new DateTime(2026, 1, 2) has Kind = Unspecified, which is not a time zone but the absence of one. Nothing goes wrong while the value is only compared with others of the same unstated zone; it goes wrong where something turns it into a fixed moment, because that conversion takes the missing offset from whichever machine is running. ⚠ The two conversions assume opposite things about the same value: ToUniversalTime() treats an Unspecified value as local and subtracts the machine's offset, ToLocalTime() treats it as UTC and adds it. One value, one Kind, two contradictory readings — which is why round-tripping correctly on the author's machine is not evidence of anything, and why the failure surfaces in one region, twice a year, in rows another process wrote.

Example

Instead of:

var starts = new DateTime(2026, 3, 29, 2, 30, 0);
record.StartsAtUtc = starts.ToUniversalTime();

Write:

var starts = new DateTimeOffset(2026, 3, 29, 2, 30, 0, TimeSpan.Zero);
record.StartsAtUtc = starts.UtcDateTime;

When it does not fire

⚠ The rule reports the escape, never the value, because reporting every `DateTime` would be absurd. A value whose zone nobody stated is not wrong while it is only compared with, formatted from or stored beside other values of the same unstated zone — that is a domain that does not model time zones, which is a decision rather than a defect. The finding is made at the one point where the value is turned into a fixed moment on the world's timeline, because that conversion has to supply an offset and takes it from whichever machine is running.

Three sinks, and only three: ToUniversalTime(), ToLocalTime(), and the DateTime-to-DateTimeOffset conversion in both its spellings — new DateTimeOffset(value) and the implicit one the compiler inserts for DateTimeOffset when = value;. ⚠ The implicit conversion needs the operation tree rather than the syntax, because DateTimeOffset when = built; contains no new and no cast; it is also the commonest spelling of the defect, so a syntax-only rule would have been silent on the majority of it. A DateTimeOffset constructor that is handed an offset is silence: an offset that was written down is the repair.

⚠ `Kind` is proved from the constructor's parameter list, never guessed, and that is what keeps the false-positive rate at zero rather than merely low. The only source treated as Unspecified is a new DateTime(…) whose overload takes no DateTimeKind — a property of the overload, so the tick-count, Calendar and TimeOnly constructors are all decided correctly without being listed. An argument spelled DateTimeKind.Unspecified is not reported: the author wrote the zone down, and the finding is about a zone nobody stated. A value arriving from a parameter, a field, a property, a parse or another assembly has a Kind nothing here can prove, and an unproved Kind is silence — which is the largest stated gap in the rule and the price of never guessing.

A local is read through only when it is assigned exactly once. The search for a second write covers the whole enclosing member, which is wider than the local's scope; seeing a write that cannot reach the local makes the rule decline, and that over-approximation is the sound direction. Assignments, ref/out arguments and increment are all writes.

⚠ No fix, and the reason is that the fix is the finding. The repair is to state which zone the value is in — DateTimeKind.Utc, DateTimeKind.Local, or a DateTimeOffset carrying a real offset — and nothing in the source says which one the author meant. An edit that picked Utc would be right about half the time and would silently change what the program means the other half, which is worse than the finding it removed.
